title: Check a skill before you trust it.
subtitle: A Claude skill can run code on your behalf. Here's what can go wrong, and the five-minute check to run first:
text: A colleague sends you a skill. "This one is great. It does our weekly reports." You download the zip. You upload it. You switch it on. It works. Everyone's happy. But you just let someone else's code run inside your Claude, with access to whatever you give it. Most skills are harmless. Some aren't. The good news: checking a skill takes about five minutes, and you don't need to be technical. Here's everything: Why a skill is more than a prompt The two real risks The five-minute check, step by step What a script should never do Ask Claude to review a skill for you What teams and companies can turn on What to do if something looks wrong Why a skill is more than a prompt A prompt is words. You read it before you send it. A skill can be more than that. Besides the SKILL.md file, a skill can carry: reference files that Claude reads when it needs them templates it fills in scripts: code that runs when Claude uses the skill And here's the part most people miss: skills load in layers. Claude reads the instructions only when a request matches, and opens the extra files only if needed. Scripts run, and only their results come back to Claude. So you might use a skill for weeks without ever seeing what's inside. Treat an unknown skill like an unknown app. You wouldn't install an app from a stranger without a second look. The two real risks 1. Prompt injection Hidden instructions that steer Claude into something you didn't ask for. They can hide anywhere in a skill's text: deep in the instructions, in a reference file, in a template. You ask for your weekly report. The skill quietly tells Claude to do something else as well. 2. Data leaks A script that sends your information somewhere. Your notes, your numbers, your files: whatever you give the skill to work on. Anthropic's advice for both risks is the same: check before you trust. The five-minute check Do this before you upload any skill you didn't write yourself. Step 1: The source (30 seconds) Who made it? Install only from sources you trust. Even a skill a colleague shares deserves a look first. They may not have checked it either. Don't know the source? Stop here. Step 2: Read SKILL.md (2 minutes) Unzip a copy of the skill on your computer. Open SKILL.md. Read it from top to bottom. Ask yourself: Does the description match the job it promises? Do the instructions stay on that job? Is there anything that tells Claude to do something unrelated, or to hide what it's doing? Step 3: Read every script (2 minutes) Look in the scripts/ folder, if there is one. You don't need to understand every line. You're looking for two things: anything that downloads software anything that sends information to a website If you see a web address in a script, ask why it's there. Step 4: Look for secrets (30 seconds) There should be no passwords, API keys or personal data in a skill. Not in the instructions, not in a file. If you find one, the skill was built carelessly. That's reason enough to stop. Step 5: Test it on something harmless Upload it. Switch it on. Try it first on files that don't matter. Does it do what it says, and only that? Then you can use it for real work. Save the full skills guide What a script should never do Scripts are useful. They're the right tool for steps that must come out the same every time: calculations, format checks, conversions. But a script for those jobs has no reason to: download software send information to a website read files you didn't give it contain passwords or keys A script that formats a report doesn't need the internet. If it reaches out to a website, ask why before you switch the skill on. Here's a useful comparison. Every skill in the library I wrote for the people I teach is plain text you can read in a minute. Only three files are scripts, and they use only Python's standard library and never connect to the internet. That's the bar. Hold every skill to it. Get the next issue by email Ask Claude to review a skill for you Not comfortable reading code? Let Claude help. Paste the skill's files into a normal chat, with the skill switched off, and ask: I'm about to install this Claude skill. Read every file below and tell me, in plain English: 1. What the skill does. 2. Whether any instruction asks for something unrelated to that job, or hides what it's doing. 3. Whether any script downloads software, sends information to a website, or reads files it wasn't given. 4. Whether there are passwords, API keys or personal data anywhere. Quote the exact lines you're worried about. [paste the files here] Read the answer carefully. Then look at the lines it quotes yourself. This helps, but it doesn't replace your own read of the files. Hidden instructions are written to be missed. What teams and companies can turn on If your company uses Claude on a team plan, there's more you can do. Team plans: skills are on by default, so it's worth agreeing as a team which skills you trust. Enterprise plans: an owner turns skills on first, in Organization settings → Plugins & skills, on the Policy tab. Skill scanning: on Enterprise plans, owners can turn on skill scanning, which checks uploaded skills for malicious content. Keep a short shared list of the skills your team has checked, and who checked them. It saves everyone from repeating the work. If something looks wrong Don't switch it on. Already did? Open Customize → Skills and switch it off. Then: Tell whoever shared it what you found. Delete the zip from wherever you saved it. If you gave it files with personal or company data, tell the person responsible for security at your company. There's no shame in it. Checking is exactly what you're supposed to do. Questions people ask Do I need to check skills I wrote myself? Less so. But re-read anything you copied in from elsewhere: an example, a template or a script you found online. What about skills in Claude's own directory? In Customize → Skills → + → Browse skills, you'll find skills from partners such as Notion, Figma and Atlassian…

title: Ten skills worth writing.
subtitle: The ten Claude skills I wrote for the people I teach: what each one does, why it works, and a request to try:
text: People ask me the same question every week. "I get what a skill is. But what should I actually make one for?" So here's my answer, in full. These are the ten skills I wrote for the people I teach. Each one does one job, the way I'd want it done. I'll show you what each does, the rules that make it work, and a request to try. Steal the ideas. Then write your own versions, for the way you work. What's inside: Two skills for learning Two for research Two for your career Two for everyday work One for data One that writes the others How to choose your first The ten, on one page Every skill below follows the same pattern. A clear job. A few firm rules. One thing it never does. That last part matters most. A good skill isn't only what Claude does. It's what Claude refuses to do. Learn and remember learn-anything A patient tutor for any topic. It doesn't start explaining right away. First it asks what you already know. Then it makes a short plan, and explains one idea at a time, each with an analogy and a small example. Before moving on, it checks you understood. Why it works: most explanations start in the wrong place. Too basic, and you're bored. Too advanced, and you're lost. Asking first fixes both. Teach me how neural networks learn. I know basic algebra. Always say what you already know. "I know basic algebra" changes the whole explanation. quiz-me Turns your notes, a document or a topic into practice questions. It asks them one at a time. It explains every answer, keeps track of what you miss, and comes back to it. Why it works: reading notes feels like learning. Answering questions is learning. And coming back to the ones you missed is where it sticks. Quiz me on these lecture notes. Ten questions, mixed. Make your own version: the five steps Research and explain research-brief Answers a question with a one-page, sourced brief. It separates what's known from what's only claimed. It gives each finding a confidence level. And it never invents a source. Why it works: the danger with AI research isn't a wrong answer. It's a wrong answer that sounds certain. Confidence levels and real sources make the uncertainty visible. news-explainer Turns AI and tech news into a plain explainer, in four parts: What happened Why it matters Who it affects What's still unknown Every claim is attributed. No hype. Why it works: the fourth part. Most news coverage skips what isn't known yet. Naming it keeps you honest with your readers. Explain this announcement for my newsletter readers. Paste the link or the text under it. Grow your career linkedin-post Writes LinkedIn posts in your own voice, from an idea, a lesson or a piece of work. You get an opening worth reading and one clear point. What you don't get: invented stories or engagement bait. Why it works: it learns your voice from your own old posts. So the post sounds like you on a good day, not like a template. Turn this project I finished into a post. Here are two of my old posts. job-application Tailors your CV and cover letter to one specific job ad. It matches your real experience to what the employer asks for. And it tells you honestly where the gaps are. Why it works: honesty. A tailored CV that invents experience falls apart in the interview. One that tells you where you're weak gives you time to prepare. Here's my CV and the job ad. Tailor both. Get the next issue by email Get work done meeting-to-actions Turns meeting notes or a transcript into: the decisions the actions, with owners and deadlines the open questions a follow-up email, ready to send It never invents an owner or a date. Why it works: a summary nobody acts on is wasted. Owners and deadlines turn a meeting into work that gets done. And refusing to invent them means you find the gaps before they cost you. Here's the transcript of today's team call. presentation-planner Plans a talk before you open slide software: the story one message per slide titles that state the point the visuals the speaker notes Why it works: most bad decks are a planning problem, not a design problem. Fix the story first, and the slides almost write themselves. Plan a ten-minute talk on our quarterly results for the board. Work with data check-the-numbers Answers questions about spreadsheets, CSV files and SQL results, and proves the answer first. A script profiles each file before Claude answers: missing values numbers stored as text repeated rows and keys gaps in the dates Every join is checked for multiplied rows. And the answer comes with its caveats. Why it works: this is the skill where a script earns its place. Checking data must come out the same every time, and code does that better than words. Which products drove last quarter's revenue? Here's the export. When a step must be exact (a calculation, a format check, a conversion), put it in a script, not in the instructions. Make your own skill-maker The one that writes the others. It interviews you about a task you repeat. Then it writes the SKILL.md, checks it against the rules, and packages the folder as a zip, ready to upload. Why it works: the hardest part of a skill is describing your own job. Being interviewed is much easier than starting from a blank page. Help me turn the way I write our weekly report into a skill. The full walkthrough: make your first skill What a good skill looks like inside Every skill above is the same shape inside: a name, a description, and short, firm instructions. Here's how learn-anything could look, so you can see the pattern: --- name: learn-anything description: Teaches any topic step by step, starting from what the learner already knows. Use when someone asks to learn, understand or be taught a topic. --- ## Steps 1. Ask what I already know about the topic, and why I want to learn it. 2. Make a short plan: three to five ideas, in order. 3. Explain one idea at a time, with an analogy and a small example. 4. Ask one question to check I understood before moving on. ## Mistakes to avoid - Don't explain everything in…

title: Make your first skill.
subtitle: Turn the instructions you paste into Claude every day into a skill that does the job your way:
text: Every morning, the same ritual. You open Claude. You paste the same long block of instructions. You explain the format again. The tone. The headings. The thing it got wrong yesterday. Then you correct the same mistakes. There's a better way, and it takes about an hour, once. You teach Claude the job one time, in a skill. From then on, Claude picks it up by itself whenever a request needs it. No pasting. No re-explaining. Your way, every time. Here's everything you need to make your first one: Know when a task deserves a skill Pick the right first task Understand what's inside a skill Write the SKILL.md, and the line that matters most Write the instructions Add templates and scripts (only if you need them) Zip it the right way Upload it and test it with five requests Fix it when Claude doesn't use it Know when a task deserves a skill Not everything should be a skill. Claude already gives you three other ways to shape how it works. Each one fits a different need: Custom instructions hold your general preferences. They apply to every conversation. Projects hold background documents and knowledge. They apply to the chats inside that project. Connectors give Claude access to other apps and data, such as your drive or calendar, when it needs them. A skill is a way of doing one particular job. It applies only when a request needs it, in any chat. My rule is simple. Once you've explained the same thing to Claude three times, make it a skill. Once is a one-off. Twice is a coincidence. Three times is a job, and jobs deserve skills. Skills and connectors work well together. A connector lets Claude reach your project tracker; a skill teaches it how your team writes tickets. Not sure what a skill is? Start with the guide Pick the right first task Your first skill should be boring. That's a compliment. Boring jobs are the ones you repeat, and the ones you repeat are where a skill pays off fastest. Good first tasks The weekly report your manager expects in a fixed format. The summary you write after every client meeting. The email you send in your team's tone, again and again. The checklist you run before you send anything important. Tasks to leave for later A job you do once a quarter. You won't remember to use it. A job that is really three jobs. Split it, or the skill will do all three badly. A job you can't describe yet. If you can't explain it to a colleague, you can't explain it to Claude. One skill, one job. If you need two jobs, make two skills. Throughout this issue, I'll use one example: a weekly report. Understand what's inside a skill A skill is just a folder. It has one required file, SKILL.md, and a few optional ones: weekly-report/ ├── SKILL.md required: name, description and instructions ├── reference.md optional: detail Claude reads only when it needs it ├── templates/ optional: files to fill in └── scripts/ optional: code for steps that must be exact That's the whole thing. No app to build. No code to write, unless you want to. Why you can have many skills Skills load in layers. Always: Claude sees just the name and description of every skill you've switched on. A line or two each. When a request matches: Claude reads that skill's instructions. Only if needed: it opens the extra files. Scripts run, and only their results come back. So ten skills don't slow Claude down. Each one costs a line or two until the moment it's needed. This is also why the description matters so much. Most of the time, it's the only part of your skill Claude sees. Write the SKILL.md Make a folder named after your skill: weekly-report. Inside it, make a file called SKILL.md. It starts with a name and a description, between two lines of dashes: --- name: weekly-report description: Turns the week's notes and numbers into our team's weekly report format. Use when someone asks for the weekly report or pastes weekly updates. --- The name Lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens only. 64 characters at most. The same as the folder's name. It can't contain "claude" or "anthropic". The name is also the command you can type, like /weekly-report. The description: the line that matters most Claude decides when to use your skill from the description alone. Write it badly, and your skill sits there unused. Write it well, and Claude reaches for it at the right moment, every time. A strong description does two things: Says what the skill does. Says when to use it. Write it in the third person ("Turns the week's notes...", not "I help you..."). Keep it to 200 characters in the Claude apps (the API allows 1,024). No tags in angle brackets. Compare these two: Helps with reports. Turns the week's notes and numbers into our team's weekly report format. Use when someone asks for the weekly report or pastes weekly updates. The first one could mean anything. The second one tells Claude exactly when to step in. Get the next guide by email Write the instructions Below the dashes comes the job itself. Write it the way you'd brief a sharp new colleague on their first day. Keep it under 500 lines, and include four things: Numbered steps. What to do, in order. The mistakes to avoid. The ones Claude made last time. One short example. A good finished result. A checklist, if the job is long. Here's how the weekly report skill could start: ## Steps 1. Read the notes and numbers I paste. 2. Group them under: Wins, Numbers, Risks, Next week. 3. Keep each point to one line. 4. Put the three numbers that changed most at the top of Numbers. ## Mistakes to avoid - Don't invent numbers. If one is missing, write [missing]. - Don't add a greeting or a sign-off. ## Example (paste one report you were happy with) Your best example is a real one. Paste a report you were proud of, with anything private removed. Let Claude draft it with you Don't want to start from a blank page? Ask Claude to interview you first: Help me turn the way I write our weekly report into a skill. Ask me questions first, then write the SKILL.md. Answer its questions honestly. Then…

title: Claude skills, from zero.
subtitle: For anyone who pastes the same instructions into Claude every day: install your first skill safely and use it today.
text: You paste the same long instructions into Claude. You explain the same format again. You correct the same mistakes. A skill ends that. You teach Claude a job once, and it does it your way from then on. By the end of this guide you'll have: one skill installed and switched on a clear idea of when Claude uses it a short safety check you can run on any skill You need: a Claude account and ten minutes. 1. Know what a skill is A skill is a small folder of instructions. Sometimes it also holds scripts and templates. Every skill has one required file: SKILL.md. Its first lines hold two things: a name, which is also the command you can type, such as /learn-anything a description of what the skill does and when to use it Below that come the instructions: steps, rules, examples and checklists. Claude decides when to use a skill from its description alone. A clear description is the difference between a skill that works and one that sits there. 2. See how skills differ You already have other ways to shape Claude. Here's where a skill fits: Feature What it gives Claude When it applies Custom instructions Your general preferences Every conversation Projects Background documents and knowledge Chats inside that project Connectors (MCP) Access to other apps and data When Claude needs that app Skills A way of doing one job Only when a request needs it, in any chat They work well together. A connector lets Claude reach your project tracker. A skill teaches it how your team writes tickets. 3. Check where skills work Skills work in more places than most people think: Claude on the web and in the desktop app, on every plan from Free to Enterprise, once code execution is on. Claude Code, from folders on your computer. Claude for Excel, PowerPoint, Word and Outlook. Cowork, which uses the skills switched on for your account. The Claude API, in beta, where skills run in a sandbox with no internet access. Skills also follow an open standard, the Agent Skills specification. A skill you write isn't locked to one product. 4. Turn skills on Open Settings → Capabilities. Turn on Create and edit files. In the older Settings layout, it's called Code execution and file creation. On Team plans, skills are on by default. On Enterprise plans, an owner turns them on first, in Organization settings → Plugins & skills, on the Policy tab. 5. Install a skill There are two ways to get one. Ready-made: open Customize → Skills, click +, then Browse skills. You'll find skills from partners such as Notion, Figma and Atlassian, built to work with their connectors. From a zip (one you made, or one from a source you trust): Get the skill's zip file. Don't unzip it. Open Customize → Skills, click +, then Create skill → Upload a skill. Choose the zip. Check that the skill's switch is on. That's it. Ask for something the skill covers. Make your own skill 6. Use it You rarely need to do anything special. Claude reads the descriptions of your skills and uses one by itself when your request matches. To be sure, name it: Use my weekly-report skill on these notes. In Claude Code and in the Microsoft 365 add-ins, you can also type / and pick a skill from the list. Claude didn't use the skill you expected? Check that its switch is on, name it in your request, or make its description clearer about when it applies. 7. Add skills to Claude Code Claude Code reads skills from folders on your computer. For every project: unzip the skill into ~/.claude/skills/, so you end up with ~/.claude/skills/learn-anything/SKILL.md. For one project (and everyone who works on it): unzip it into the project's .claude/skills/ folder and commit it. Run a skill by typing a slash and its name, or just ask. /skills lists what's installed. Skills you switch on in your Claude account also sync to Claude Code when you sign in with the same account. Find skills worth installing There are three good places to start. 1. Claude's own directory. In Customize → Skills, click +, then Browse skills. You'll find skills from partners such as Notion, Figma and Atlassian, built to work with their connectors. 2. Anthropic's examples. At github.com/anthropics/skills. Good to learn from, and to adapt to the way you work. 3. Your own. The best skills capture the tasks you repeat every week, the way your organisation does them. Nobody else can write those for you. issue:ten-skills-worth-writing Make your own Once you've explained the same thing to Claude three times, it's worth a skill. The short version: Make a folder named after the job, like weekly-report. Write SKILL.md: a name and a description between two lines of dashes, then numbered steps, the mistakes to avoid and one short example. Zip the folder, not the files inside it. Upload it in Customize → Skills, and switch it on. Test it with three requests that should use it and two that shouldn't. The full walkthrough: make your first skill 8. Stay safe A skill can contain code that runs when Claude uses it. So treat an unknown skill like an unknown app. Never put passwords, API keys or personal data in a skill. The two main risks: Prompt injection: hidden instructions that steer Claude into something you didn't ask for. Data leaks: a script that sends your information somewhere. The fix is the same for both: check before you trust. On Enterprise plans, owners can also turn on skill scanning, which checks uploaded skills for malicious content.
